To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
average emotional responses to negative life events increase across most of the life span, but the magnitude of individual differences in such responses is greatest in midlife.

(a) average daily stress reactivity increases with age and is highest in old age, (b) daily stress reactivity is relatively stable over time, but this stability declines in old age, and (c) daily stress reactivities vary across time, with higher daily stress reactivity occurring when individuals report higher global stress.

(1) the within-person relationship between daily stress and negative emotions increased with age, (2) individual differences in the relationship between daily stress, and negative emotions were relatively stable over time, but this stability decreased in older age, and (3) the relationship between daily life stress and negative emotions was stronger during periods when individuals were experiencing high levels of chronic stress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of stress and emotion across the adult lifespan.
the role that daily stress plays in the aging process.
how the stress process is experienced and regulated across the lifespan.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is little longitudinal information about aging-related changes in the emotional responses to negative life events.
the present results emphasize that it is important to study the dynamic nature of stress processes across the adult life span.
aging is a process that is characterized by a complex set of dynamic changes in multiple biological, psychological, and social systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aging process is a dynamic process that is not uniform across time and that it is important to consider how the dynamic nature of aging may influence daily stress processes and health outcomes.

aging is associated with an increased reactivity to daily events and that individual differences in this reactivity are stable across the lifespan, although this stability is not as strong in old age as it is in midlife.

the within-person coupling between daily stress and negative emotions increases in late adulthood, and this increase may reflect an age-related increase in the sensitivity of negative emotional responding to the daily stress process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

aging-related changes in stress reactivity and stability of individual differences in stress reactivity can be better understood by considering the dynamic interplay between within-person and between-person processes that operate across multiple time scales.
aging is not simply a process of gradual deterioration, but also a process of change that can involve both gains and losses.
the way people respond to daily stress is not fixed over time.
